Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 116 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
A
lberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 116 (Seven 
Persons) is located generally southwest of Medicine 
Hat and covers an area of 2,096 km2. The majority of 
the unit is within Alberta’s dry mixed-grass natural 
subregion, with the southeast portion adjacent to 
Cypress Hills extending into the mixed-grass natural 
subregion. Several drainages containing large coulee 
systems originate in the Cypress Hills and extend 
westward and northward through the WMU, including 
Peigan Creek, Bullshead Creek, and Seven Persons 
Creek. Land is primarily deeded, and general habitat 
and land use consists of cultivated cropland for the 
purpose of annual crop production, and tame and 
native grassland used for cattle grazing. Some parcels 
of crown owned native grassland under grazing lease 
are also present. Oil and gas development is 
established throughout the WMU, and in recent years, 
renewable energy development has also increased. 
Chronic Wasting Disease is now well established 
within the WMU, with 80 positives since first detected 
in 2015 (https://open.alberta.ca/publications/chronic-
wasting-disease-in-alberta-by-wildlife-management-
unit). Submitted samples from 2023 indicate 
prevalence rates of 33% in mule deer and 52% of 25 
mule deer bucks tested positive for the disease. 
A
 WMU 116 survey for mule deer, white-tailed deer, 
and moose was last conducted in 2024 using strip-
transect methodology (https://www.alberta.ca/aerial-
wildlife-survey-reports) . The 2024 and 2025 surveys 
of WMU 116 with consistent methodology and flight 
dates provide an excellent opportunity to evaluate 
annual demographic change and supported the 
Alberta Mule Deer Collaring Project 
(https://www.apos.ab.ca/media).  
T
he objective of the February 2025 survey was to 
assess the status of deer, moose, and elk in WMU 116 
with estimates for abundance and age-sex 
composition. We also scanned for collared mule deer 
and recorded observations of additional species of 
game management or conservation concern including 
elk, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive 
or at-risk species.
S
urvey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 8–11, 2025 flying 44 east-west 
lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 50% coverage (800 m 
wide survey strip, area surveyed 1043 km2) and a total 
linear survey effort of 1304 km. At each observation 
point, ungulates were classified by species, and when 
possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on 
one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more 
points; antlers inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 
points, antlers outside of ears).  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose 
was calculated by multiplying the number of animals 
per transect (∑x) by total area (km2) searched (total 
survey strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 1969, as described in 
Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area (km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with 90% confidence intervals. Confidence 
interval width was calculated by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-
distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number 
of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as 
the number of transects sampled. 
Elk observations were recorded as a minimum total 
count (MTC) within the WMU. 
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 828 mule deer were observed with an 
average groups size of 11.5 (range 1-52). The 
estimated density was 0.79 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 1,662 individuals (90% CI 
1,012 – 2,312). A total of 728 mule deer were 
successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio 
was estimated to be 21:100:69. That results in an 
estimated 2025 winter mule deer population of 184 
bucks, 875 does, and 603 fawns. Of the 79 mule deer 
bucks classified, 22 (28%) were classified ‘small’, 38

(48%) ‘medium’, and 19 (24%) ‘large’. No collared 
mule deer were observed during the survey. 
The 2025 mule deer survey results indicate stable 
abundance from 2024, but with differences in 
distribution and demographics. Average group size in 
2025 was more than twice that observed in 2024, as 
was maximum group size, indicating a more clumped 
distribution and reducing the 2025 abundance 
estimate precision. While fawn:doe ratios were similar 
and high (69:100 in 2025; 78:100 in 2024) indicating 
good recruitment, there was a marked decline in 
buck:doe ratios (21:100 in 2025; 49:100 in 2024). 
Further, the proportions of antler size classifications in 
mule deer shifted to younger bucks (24% “large” in 
2025; 33% “large in 2024). While some of the 
differences between buck:doe ratios and antler size 
classifications could be attributed to annual variation in 
timing of antler drop, they are consistent with sex and 
age specific CWD prevalence and mortality rates. 
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 780 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 15.9 (range 1-108). The 
estimated density was 0.75 deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 1,566 individuals (90% CI 
1072 – 2059). A total of 288 white-tailed deer were 
successfully classified. The buck:doe:fawn ratio was 
estimated to be 8:100:70. That results in an estimated 
2025 early winter white-tailed deer population of 70 
bucks, 880 does, and 616 fawns. 
The 2025 white-tailed deer survey results indicate a 
260% increase in abundance. Such a dramatic 
increase in abundance cannot be accounted for solely 
by intrinsic growth rate and must indicate significant 
immigration of white-tailed deer into WMU 116 from 
surrounding units. White-tailed deer exhibited the 
same increase in average group size as mule deer 
between the 2024 and 2025 surveys, possibly 
influenced by heavy snowfall in the unit late January 
through early February. The extremely low buck:doe 
ratio (8:100 2025; 24:100), and observations of 
“unicorn” bucks, indicate antler drop was advanced in 
2025 compared to 2024, but could also be a result of 
immigration by does/fawns. Antlerless bucks classified 
as does would decrease both the buck and fawn:doe 
ratios. 
Incidental observations 
 A total of 21 moose were observed (six bull, nine cow, 
five calf, one unclassified). The estimated density was 
0.02 moose/km2 and the estimated abundance was 42 
individuals (90% CI 22 – 63). Moose were generally 
confined to brushy creek valleys and associated 
coulees as suitable moose habitat is generally limited 
in prairie WMUs. There may have been a small 
increase in moose abundance between 2024 and 
2025, but confidence intervals are overlapping. 
One elk and 526 pronghorn were observed during the 
survey. Other species observations include sharp-
tailed grouse, gray partridge, ring-necked pheasant, 
bald eagle, and coyote.
